Ce sont ces mots dont nous séparons la voyelle finale par le signe /. Si, au contraire, l'accent porte sur la voyelle finale, le mot ne subit aucune altération. Ex : gon/o, enfant, petit; bis/i, chien; pusa, beau; gonbis pusa t'ilada, un très beau petit chien. [p. 9-10:] Si l'on considère les mots de la forme kag/a, dans lesquels l'accent porte sur la première voyelle, on remarque que, dans la majorité des cas, la voyelle finale est la même que la voyelle accentuée.
new_statements.translation: 2° When a word is inside a clause, or inside a compound, or carries a suffix, if the accent does not fall on its final vowel, that vowel disappears. These are the words whose final vowel we separate with the sign /. If, on the contrary, the accent falls on the final vowel, the word undergoes no alteration. E.g. gon/o 'child, small'; bis/i 'dog'; pusa 'beautiful'; gonbis pusa t'ilada 'a very beautiful little dog'. [pp. 9-10:] If one considers words of the kag/a type, in which the accent falls on the first vowel, one notices that in most cases the final vowel is the same as the accented vowel.

new_statements.relation_note: ' = fixed final) is not what Gaden says: he describes two lexical classes, accent on the first vowel (kag/a, gon/o, bis/i) versus accent on the final vowel (pusa, kaga), with class membership marked per word; only the second clause of his 2° law mentions final-vowel accent. So the placement is lexical, not fixed: final syllable. This agrees with the webcat data record for bagi1246 (catalog_kind 'lexical', same p. 9 quotation) and with its check note that StressTyp2's 'final' gloss over-reads Gaden. new_statements.rule_in_words: Gaden gives no placement rule. Disyllabic words fall into two lexical classes: those accented on the first vowel (kag/a 'tree', gon/o 'child', bis/i 'dog'), which lose their final vowel when not phrase-final or when suffixed, and those accented on the final vowel (pusa 'beautiful', kaga 'leopard'), which are invariable. Membership is marked word by word with the sign / (p. 8: 'Le signe / placé en avant d'une voyelle, indique que cette voyelle disparaît dès que le mot n'est pas isolé ou en finale. Exemple : kag/a, arbre; kag muta, trois arbres. Quand ce signe est absent, le mot est invariable : kaga, panthère'). Accent is thus contrastive and lexically distributed between initial and final vowel, not fixed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned. p. 8 also notes a diacritic marking 'sur les voyelles initiales de quelques mots, une accentuation spéciale, qui n'est pas une aspiration' (a special accentuation on the initial vowels of some words, not an aspiration).
new_statements.exceptions: Loi 4° notes that isolated/final words generally end in a vowel with exceptions (Kapam! vs Malama), which Gaden attributes to 'une tendance au moindre effort appliquée à des intonations différentes'. He observes that kag/a-type words (first-vowel accent) rarely surface in full because of suffixes and the determiner na, and speculates the final vowel assimilated to the accented one.
new_statements.identity_note: Gaden 1909: 4 (Introduction, Rosetta detail-1 excerpt): 'Le dialecte que nous avons étudié est celui de Massenya, qui est le « Tar Bɔnna » proprement dit.. Les dialectes du Koubar et des villages riverains du Chari n'en diffèrent d'ailleurs que par quelques mots' — the description is of the Massenya dialect, checked with the private secretary of Sultan Gaourang. The bundled English typescript is a later description (post-Gaden, 'my informant'), unattributed in the scan; the catalog identifies it with Stevenson 1969.

new_statements.translation: — The sign / placed before a vowel indicates that this vowel disappears as soon as the word is not isolated or final. Example: kag/a 'tree'; kag muta 'three trees'. When this sign is absent, the word is invariable: kaga 'leopard'; kaga muta 'three leopards'.

readall_conflicts: '). Gaden's 'Lois phonétiques' 2° sets up two lexical classes — words accented on the first vowel (kag/a 'tree', gon/o 'child', bis/i 'dog'), whose final vowel drops in non-final or suffixed position, and words accented on the final vowel (pusa 'beautiful', kaga 'leopard'), which are invariable — and marks the class per word with the sign /; nothing in the text makes final accent the general case. StressTyp2's 'final' reading rests on the second clause of that law alone. The project's own webcat data record for bagi1246 already codes the language 'lexical' from the same quotation and flags the StressTyp2 reading as an over-reading, so the disagreement is between StressTyp2 and the source, not between sources. A second document bundled in the same Rosetta scan (unattributed typescript 'Notes on Phonetics of Bagirmi', p. 16) describes the language as tri-tonal (High, Mid, Low) and has no stress section; it does not contradict Gaden, it is silent on stress.
